## How the Sun Works

### Panel A — Solar Activity Now

- **Purpose / 5E connection:** Engage + Explore. Put a real-time measurement of
  the Sun's X-ray output in front of students before the "How the Sun works"
  lesson.
- **What students see:** A log-scale graph of NOAA GOES X-ray flux (0.1–0.8 nm)
  over 24 or ~72 hours, with A/B/C/M/X flare-class reference bands, the latest
  value, and the window peak.
- **What the data mean:** The quiet Sun sits near the B/C boundary; flares spike
  the curve by one or more class letters. The X-ray flux reflects magnetic
  activity in the Sun's corona, not total energy output.
- **Classification:** <span class="obs">Observed</span> — GOES satellite
  measurement, W/m².
- **Two-minute phenomenon question (Think–Talk–Open Exchange):** *"Why does this
  line stay flat for hours and then jump in a few minutes?"*
- **Longer investigation:** Track the peak value over several days; have students
  argue whether the Sun is "steady" using the Claim–Evidence–Reasoning scaffold.
- **Teacher look-fors:** Students reading the log scale correctly; students
  distinguishing flux (this panel) from total solar irradiance (not this panel).
- **Misconceptions & limitations:** X-ray flux ≠ total solar irradiance; a flare
  class letter is a logarithmic band, not a linear step; the graph is a
  satellite measurement, not a camera picture.
- **Accessibility/MLL supports:** Provide the flare-class letters verbally;
  pair numeric values with the colored bands; use the text readouts alongside
  the graph.
- **Troubleshooting:** If NOAA data does not load, the panel shows an explicit
  error state (no cached copy is silently substituted). Refresh after 5 minutes.

## Star Life Cycles

### Panel E — Meet the Host Star

- **Purpose / 5E connection:** Explain + Elaborate. Connect an exoplanet's
  environment to the properties of its star on the H–R diagram.
- **What students see:** Host-star temperature, mass, radius, and luminosity
  compared with the Sun, plotted on a conventional H–R diagram (temperature
  decreasing left→right, luminosity increasing upward) with reference stars.
- **What the data mean:** A star's position on the H–R diagram tells students
  its class (main sequence, giant, white dwarf) and therefore its life stage.
- **Classification:** <span class="cat">Catalog</span> values from the NASA
  Exoplanet Archive; <span class="calc">derived</span> luminosity is clearly
  labeled (Stefan–Boltzmann, blackbody assumption); reference stars are
  published values for orientation.
- **Two-minute phenomenon question:** *"Why does a tiny, dim red star live far
  longer than a bright blue one?"*
- **Longer investigation (Domino Discover):** Sort reference stars from hottest
  to coolest, then predict their relative lifetimes.
- **Teacher look-fors:** Students reading axis direction correctly; students not
  equating "bright" with "hot and blue" incorrectly.
- **Misconceptions & limitations:** Luminosity is not temperature alone; this
  panel is catalog-backed — it is not a real-time stellar life-cycle feed; we do
  not infer precise ages here.
- **Accessibility/MLL supports:** Label star type in words next to symbols; no
  essential information is color-only.
- **Troubleshooting:** If a host star lacks a catalog luminosity, the panel shows
  "not in catalog" and only the derived value is labeled as derived.

## Planets and Orbits

### Panel B — Solar System Now

- **Purpose / 5E connection:** Explore. A top-down heliocentric view that shows
  real elliptical orbits and lets students compare any date.
- **What students see:** Selectable planets, orbital paths, today's marker,
  date + comparison date, and a table of Sun distances in AU.
- **What the data mean:** Planets move faster near perihelion; the comparison
  date shows how much each planet moves in a given interval.
- **Classification:** <span class="calc">Calculated</span> — Meeus low-precision
  ephemerides (not live telescope observations), heliocentric ecliptic frame,
  viewed from ecliptic north. Sizes and distances are **not** to scale.
- **Two-minute phenomenon question:** *"Which planet changes its distance from
  the Sun the most over one month?"*
- **Longer investigation:** Compare Mercury and Mars over a year; ask students to
  explain the difference using orbital eccentricity.
- **Teacher look-fors:** Students connecting eccentricity to distance range;
  students reading AU values, not pixel distances.
- **Misconceptions & limitations:** This is a calculated model, not a photograph;
  planet dot sizes are symbolic.
- **Accessibility/MLL supports:** The distance table is a text alternative to the
  map; planet colors are redundant with names.
- **Troubleshooting:** No network needed — positions are computed in-browser.

### Panel C — Earth vs. Comet Borrelly

- **Purpose / 5E connection:** Engage + Explore. The unit anchor phenomenon: why
  does Borrelly periodically release vaporized water and dust?
- **What students see:** Orbital comparison (Earth vs. Borrelly, ecliptic
  projection) and a synchronized Sun-distance-vs-time graph with a date slider,
  plus perihelion/aphelion values.
- **What the data mean:** As the comet approaches perihelion (≈1.3 AU), solar
  heating increases and outgassing intensifies; at aphelion (≈5.9 AU) it is
  frozen and quiet.
- **Classification:** <span class="calc">Calculated / predicted</span> — two-body
  Keplerian propagation from JPL osculating elements. This dashboard does **not**
  measure the comet's water release, and Earth's Sun distance does **not** cause
  Earth's seasons.
- **Two-minute phenomenon question:** *"What changes for the comet between
  aphelion and perihelion that could make it 'turn on'?"*
- **Longer investigation:** Drive the date slider through a perihelion passage and
  have students predict where the tail would be brightest and why.
- **Teacher look-fors:** Students linking distance to heating, not seasons.
- **Misconceptions & limitations:** The orbit shown is the ecliptic projection
  (Borrelly's orbit is inclined ~29°); positions are predictions, not
  observations; the comet is small and faint — not visible to the unaided eye.
- **Accessibility/MLL supports:** The synchronized graph provides the same
  information in a non-spatial format.
- **Troubleshooting:** Elements are bundled; the two-body model is approximate
  and does not include outgassing forces.

### Panel D — Earth–Exoplanet Comparison

- **Purpose / 5E connection:** Evaluate. Use real catalog data to answer "which
  exoplanet is most Earth-like?" — while resisting a single score.
- **What students see:** A size comparison of Earth and a selected exoplanet,
  plus radius, mass, orbital period, eccentricity, equilibrium temperature,
  host-star properties, discovery info, and distance.
- **What the data mean:** Many "Earth-sized" planets orbit stars very unlike the
  Sun; equilibrium temperature is a no-atmosphere model estimate, not a surface
  temperature.
- **Classification:** <span class="cat">Catalog</span> — NASA Exoplanet Archive
  `pscomppars` table, with retrieval date and provenance shown.
- **Two-minute phenomenon question:** *"Which single number best measures
  'Earth-like' — radius, temperature, or something else?"*
- **Longer investigation (Class Consensus Discussion):** Have teams defend one
  planet as "most Earth-like," then identify what evidence is still missing.
- **Teacher look-fors:** Students citing units (R⊕, M⊕, K, AU); students
  treating missing values as missing, not zero.
- **Misconceptions & limitations:** No habitability or Earth-likeness score is
  computed; resembling Earth in radius does not make a planet habitable;
  equilibrium temperature ≠ measured surface temperature.
- **Accessibility/MLL supports:** The table provides a text alternative to the
  size circles; missing values are shown explicitly.
- **Troubleshooting:** The default dataset is a curated 16-planet snapshot;
  a search box filters that list. Live catalog search requires the optional
  backend (see Hub README).

## Optional local sky observation

### Panel F — Tonight's Observing Targets

- **Purpose / 5E connection:** Extend. Bring orbital geometry down to the
  student's local horizon.
- **What students see:** Altitude, azimuth, predicted magnitude, above/below
  horizon status, a sky-direction view, and a table for a configurable location
  and evening time.
- **What the data mean:** A planet can be above the horizon yet unobservable in
  daylight or twilight; the panel reports the Sun's altitude so you can decide.
- **Classification:** <span class="calc">Calculated</span> — observer ephemerides
  (Meeus) with approximate magnitudes. No browser geolocation is requested; the
  initial location is configurable.
- **Two-minute phenomenon question:** *"Why can Venus be above the horizon right
  now and still be invisible?"*
- **Longer investigation (outdoor option):** Use the Field Journal (below) to
  record one target's altitude and azimuth at two times, then explain the change.
- **Teacher look-fors:** Students distinguishing "above horizon" from
  "visible"; students reading azimuth from North.
- **Misconceptions & limitations:** Above horizon ≠ visible; this panel never
  gives solar-viewing guidance; magnitudes are approximate.
- **Accessibility/MLL supports:** The table is the primary text alternative to
  the sky chart.
- **Troubleshooting:** Enter your location in Settings (⚙) on the dashboard.

## Constructed-response scaffold

<div class="scaffold">
<strong>1 · Describe the pattern.</strong> What do the data show changing, and
over what interval?<br>
<strong>2 · State a claim.</strong> Answer the question in one sentence.<br>
<strong>3 · Cite numeric evidence.</strong> Quote at least one value with its
unit (e.g., "flux rose from 1.2×10⁻⁶ to 3.4×10⁻⁵ W/m²").<br>
<strong>4 · Link to a mechanism.</strong> Explain how a system interaction
(e.g., solar heating, gravitational pull, orbital speed) produces the pattern.
</div>

## Field Journal (optional outdoor observation)

1. Record date, time, location, and timezone.
2. Identify one planet using Panel F's altitude/azimuth values.
3. Sketch the horizon with N/E/S/W labeled; mark the planet.
4. Estimate its altitude with a fist (≈10° per fist at arm's length).
5. Note sky conditions and whether the planet was actually visible.
6. Explain one way your observation matched or differed from the dashboard's
   calculated position.
